# Abstract

This project observed differences in biodiversity along the shoreline to understand the impact of the different kinds of coastal armoring. This data includes transect data along the north, west, and south sides of Moorea coastline. While Kayaking around the islands, every 20 minutes, ISP 2026 students took a 21-meter transect perpendicular to the coast to record substrate types at each meter. We identified substrates such as live coral, dead coral, coral rubble, macro-algae, turf, sand, mud, and beachrock.

## Abstract

This procedure is used for coastal monitoring and has been tested along the majority of the coastline of Moʻorea, French Polynesia, by UC Berkeley’s Island Sustainability classes. Data collection methods include surveys conducted on foot along Route de Ceinture, by kayak, and via small motorized boat. This protocol outlines standardized approaches for collecting observational data on birds, coastal armoring, boats, and substrate along shoreline transects. Through this data collection, we aim to identify relationships between human use of coastal protection structures and activities, and their effects on shoreline environments.

## Guidelines

- Do not trample coral. - Do not walk through private property, unless you have explicit authorization. - Write observations in a field notebook. - Take pictures to document your transect. - Try interacting with people as soon as possible and explaining what you are doing/getting feedback.

## Materials

- Gaia GPS mobile app - Field notebooks - Stopwatch (with seconds) - Water-appropriate shoes - Tape-measurer - Pencil

## Safety warnings

- Eels and stone fish may be present - Remain wary of stray dogs (staying grouped and pretending to pick up a stone or stick to throw at them is a sufficient deterrent) - Entering private property often happens by accident, be prepared with phrases in the local language to explain who you are

## Before start

- Wear attire appropriate for constant re-entry into the water. - Check that a working seconds stopwatch is present.. - Ensure each kayak has 2 people to properly measure transects.

## GAIA GPS Tracking

1 Have two team-members start a track on GAIA GPS. Make sure both members have full battery.

## GAIA GPS Tracking

2 At the same time that you start the track recording with the GAIA app, take a picture of the group's hand-watch with seconds starting track recording, with the GAIA-App take a picture of the group’s hand-watch with seconds showing on the hand-watch (will help make sure time on watch and GPS time are synced).

3 When done tracking, save and export the track as a .gpx file.

## Birds

4 When you see a bird, record the number and identify whether the bird(s) is an egret or heron. Refer to the bird ID sheet, linked here.

5 Record the timestamp at the time you spotted the bird.

## Coastal Monitoring

6 Take note of the time-stamp in your notes soon as the coastal profile changes or as soon as you are no longer able to monitor.

7 Record the coast types on the data sheet using the following categories: unArmored (no apparent human-made alteration), armRocks (armored coast w/ piles of rocks/stones), armSeaWall (armored coast cement/concrete wall), and armOther (other category of armored coast). When you encounter a perpendicular structure (dock/over-water bungalow/stone alignment), record a time-stamp and the type of perpendicular structure on the data sheet.

# Abstract

In an effort to better understand the pressures the Mo’orea lagoon faces, the 2026 Island Sustainability Program conducted this project to measure the presence of fishing and other boats in the lagoon to estimate their level of impact on coastal disturbance. In collaboration with Jean Wencelius from CRIOBE and Irwin Oito, a local fisherman, the data was collected over two days in early March 2026 from a small fishing boat, launching from Ma'atea and Vaianae in the south side of Mo’orea. 2-3 observers participated in collecting the data with the use of the Gaia navigation tool. Type of boat, number of people, and fishing gear used (if applicable) were recorded within the lagoon with the aim to better understand coastal disturbance in Mo’orea.

Abstract: Durability—the resistance to both fracture and degradation—is critical for the

long-term performance of soft materials and a sustainable society. Fracture resistance of soft

materials is typically enhanced through energy dissipation via the rupture of sacrificial chemical

or physical networks. These dissipation processes inevitably introduce internal damage,

compromising resistance to degradation and fundamentally limiting material lifetime. Here, we

report a universal strategy to achieve exceptional durability and ultralong operation lifetimes in

soft materials by enhancing fracture resistance through an elastic mechanism without bond scission.

Specifically, we design an elastic supramolecular sponge (ESS) that self-assemble, uniformly

disperse, and interlink with polymer networks. Upon stretch, ESSs deform adaptively and

selectively in response to tension on polymer chains, homogenizing the tension. Consequently,

fracture strength, toughness, and fatigue threshold are simultaneously increased without

compromising elasticity. For example, 90% of strength retains over 105 cycles, which is a 100-

fold increase over conventional elastomers. Our strategy is applicable across diverse materials and

enables rapid fabrication of durable 3D architectures. Our work offers a viable pathway to

improving the long-term durability and extending lifetimes of soft materials, providing a basis for

designing more sustainable polymer systems.


<!-- Page 5 -->


3

The demand for soft materials is rapidly increasing due to their broad applicability, ranging

from emerging applications such as wearable and implantable devices, soft robotics, and

bioprinting to high-volume applications including tires, dampers, and seals1-3. Accordingly, the

development of soft materials with prolonged service lifetimes is essential to reduce waste

generation and improve sustainability. To date, high fracture resistance has been considered as the

primary indicator of long service lifetime in soft materials. However, although fracture-resistant

materials can prevent complete failure under high-strain loading or withstand cyclic loading at low

strain, they still suffer from progressive performance degradation such as strength loss and

irreversible deformation even under mild cyclic conditions, ultimately necessitating frequent

replacement and increasing material waste. Therefore, soft materials with high durability—defined

as the ability to resist both fracture and degradation—are required.

Soft materials are polymer networks composed of crosslinked polymer chains. Because

crosslinking is a stochastic process, the resulting network is inherently inhomogeneous—the

lengths of polymer chains between neighboring crosslinks vary. Upon loading, this structural

inhomogeneity leads to uneven tension distribution among polymer chains4. Shorter chains bear

higher loads, reaching their maximum tension and rupturing much earlier than longer chains

(Extended Data Fig. 1)5. This sequential rupture of polymer chains, caused by network inherent

inhomogeneity6-8, progressively weakens soft materials (Fig. 1a). As a result, their durability

remains fundamentally limited, posing a critical barrier to practical use.

Recently, significant progress has been made to improve the fracture resistance of soft

materials by engineering the polymer network structure9-17. However, they often rely on inelastic

processes that degrade mechanical properties such as modulus, strength, and elasticity over

repeated cycles (Fig. 1b). For example, double networks and microgels exhibit enhanced fracture

resistance by promoting the rupture of sacrificial bonds, leading to a significant degradation of

mechanical properties over repeated cycles18,19. Elastomers filled with rigid nanoparticles exhibit

high fatigue resistance20,21, but the strain mismatch between the particles and the matrix leads to

delamination, degrading the mechanical performance22,23. Introducing supramolecular bonds into

the polymer networks has improved the fracture resistance of thermoplastic elastomers, but they

suffer from significant inelasticity due to the dissociation of supramolecules24–29. Such a

degradation of properties reduces the reliability of the material, complicates system design, and

deteriorates the overall performance. As a result, existing fracture-resistant soft materials

inevitably experience significant mechanical degradation under cyclic loading. Achieving true

durability therefore remains a fundamental challenge, as effective strategies to enhance fracture

resistance through purely elastic processes are still lacking.


<!-- Page 8 -->


6

Here, we introduce a universal approach that simultaneously enhances the resistance to

both fracture and degradation—durability—of soft materials (Fig. 1c). Specifically, we achieve

multiscale homogenization of polymer-chain tension through a fully elastic process by using

elastic, compliant mesostructures, which we call elastic supramolecular sponge (ESS) (Fig. 1d). In

a polymer network, ESSs are strongly connected to polymer chains through interpenetration and

interlinks. Between two ESSs, the polymer chains of various lengths entangle and connect the

ESSs. (Fig. 1e, left). When stretched, some shorter or more entangled polymer chains reach their

maximum stretch earlier than others. Then, they pull and deform the ESS, while other long chains

continue to stretch (Fig 1e, middle). The ESS is orders of magnitude larger than the polymer chains,

so the deformation of the ESS provides sufficient displacement to individual polymer chains. Such

selective and adaptive deformation of ESS let more polymer chains bear more loads

simultaneously (Fig. 1e, right). As a result, ESS allows the polymer network to store more energy

before fracture by homogenizing the tensions of polymer chains, enhancing fracture resistance.

In contrast to previously reported approaches for improving fracture resistance, our

approach—homogenizing the tensions of polymer chains—simultaneously enhances fracture

strength, fracture toughness and fatigue threshold while maintaining elasticity, and is broadly

applicable to polymer networks with various crosslinking densities and chemical compositions.

Furthermore, in contrast to other reported systems, our approach is less sensitive to initiator

concentration, making it compatible with light-based 3D printing technologies that require rapid

curing. Thus, our strategy not only improves the fracture resistance of polymer networks but also

enhances their processability and printability.

To form ESS, we employ a supramolecular approach by designing the structure of

oligomers (Fig. 1f). The oligomer contains three supramolecular stickers (4,4’-methylenebis


<!-- Page 9 -->


7

(phenyl urea), MPU) connected by spacer chains (poly(dimethylsiloxane), PDMS) with

interlinkers at the ends (methacrylate) (Supplementary Fig. 1). Next, the oligomers are submerged

in an ethyl acrylate (EA) precursor, where the stickers self-assemble into nanofibers through

cooperative hydrogen bondings. The hydrogen bonds are relatively strong because, when one

hydrogen bond forms, the other hydrogen bond is forced to form due to the high rigidity of the

molecular structure of MPU25,30. Since there are multiple stickers in an oligomer, an oligomer can

participate in multiple nanofibers. Consequently, oligomers form a nano-sized supramolecule held

by nanofibers. This characteristic enables the creation of deformable, compliant, and mechanically

robust mesostructures (Supplementary Fig. 2). Meanwhile, the spacer chains swell by EA,

resulting in porous supramolecules. The ESSs disperse well due to the high solubility of the spacer

chains, whereas other porous nanomaterials, such as metal organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent

organic frameworks (COFs), and zeolites, often suffer from aggregation and precipitation

(Extended Data Fig. 2). After polymerization, the ESSs and the poly(ethyl acrylate) (PEA) network

are interpenetrating and chemically interlinked (ESS-PEA).

The structure of ESS is confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) cross-

sectional images (Fig. 2a). As designed, ESSs are porous with a diameter of around 500 nm.

Considering that ESS occupies a volume approximately 103 times larger than a single PEA chain,

numerous chains will interpenetrate and chemically interlink to an ESS and participate in the

tension homogenization. When the ESS-PEA is stretched, the ESSs deform in the direction of the

stretch, as shown in the atomic force microscopy (AFM) images of the cross-section of a stretched

specimen (Fig. 2b, left). When the interfacial adhesion is weakened by removing chemical

interlinks, the ESSs do not deform under stretch (Fig. 2b, right), indicating that the tension applied

to the PEA matrix does not transmit to the ESS. Furthermore, the 2D small angle X-ray scattering

with interlinks while isotropic without interlinks, corroborating the role of interlinks (Fig. 2c). The

Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) data also supports the above observations

(Supplementary Fig. 3).

ESSs significantly enhance the fracture properties of polymer networks without

compromising elasticity. The ESS-PEA is highly stretchable and strong (stretch λ > 10 and fracture

strength ~8 MPa, Fig. 2d and e), compared to the ESS-PEA without interlinks and the pristine

highly entangled PEA (HE-PEA). This enhancement is notable considering that the pristine HE-

PEA network is a highly entangled network with a relatively high fracture resistance31. As shown

in figure 2d, HE-PEA is much stretchable and tough compared to the normal PEA, due to the effect

of entanglements that distribute tension and prevent fracture. Since the distribution of tension

through entanglements is a highly reversible process, HE-PEA also exhibits high elasticity. ESS-

PEA shows that the high fracture resistance of HE-PEA can further be amplified, without

compromising the high elasticity of HE-PEA (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 4). A notable

increase in fracture properties such as strength, work of fracture, toughness and fatigue threshold

is observed simultaneously. Furthermore, we also test the fracture properties of HE-PEA and ESS-

PEA while varying crosslinking density, since the relative number of crosslinks compared to

entanglements greatly affect mechanical properties of PEA.31 In result, the ESS-PEAs show

greater fracture strength and fatigue threshold over a wide range of crosslinking density (Extended

Data Fig. 3). The ESS-PEA shows a maximum improvement of 4.7 times in fracture strength and

4 times in fatigue threshold, compared to HE-PEA (Extended Data Fig. 4 and 5). These


<!-- Page 13 -->


11

observations suggest that the selective and large deformation of ESSs homogenizes the tension in

the polymer network, resulting in high fracture resistance. It is corroborated by the observation

that ESSs with weak interfacial adhesion do not increase fracture strength and fatigue threshold.

We also apply cyclic loading to unnotched samples to study the role of the interlink in

fatigue and elasticity (Supplementary Fig. 4 and 5). We measure the stress under cyclic loading

with a stretch of 2 and plot the stress normalized by the stress at the first cycle as a function of the

number of cycles. The pristine HE-PEA and ESS-PEA do not fracture up to 104 cycles, whereas

the ESS-PEA without interlinks exhibits a significant reduction in normalized stress and fatigue

fracture at the 150th cycle, although the stress level is lower (Fig. 2e). Also, the normalized stress

of the pristine HE-PEA and ESS-PEA plateaus at around 103 cycles with about 10% reduction

(Supplementary Fig. 4). Furthermore, residual strain of ESS-PEA shows similar value with HE-

PEA (Supplementary Fig. 5). We attribute the elasticity and high fatigue resistance of ESS-PEA

to the highly elastic deformation of ESS and strong interlinks preventing delamination between

ESS and PEA.

While numerous materials with high fracture resistance exist, most of them exhibit poor

elasticity. We compare the fracture properties—strength and fatigue threshold—of various

elastomeric materials20,31–42 (Fig. 2g,h) and gels10,31,43–46 (Extended Data Fig. 6) as a function of

hysteresis (elasticity). While previously reported approaches were effective in enhancing one of

these properties, they couldn’t improve them simultaneously. More importantly, because these

approaches rely on inelastic processes, many of the resulting materials exhibit large hysteresis.

With this unique combination of superior mechanical properties, we envisioned extending

the lifetime of elastomeric materials for practical applications. To validate this, we quantified,

under 50% tensile-strain cycling, the number of cycles required to (i) retain 90% of the initial


<!-- Page 14 -->


12

strength, (ii) retain 90% of the original dimensions, and (iii) reach 1 mm of crack growth. As shown

in Fig. 2i, the lifetime (>105 cycles) of our material surpasses that of all commercially available

high-performance elastomers. It is noteworthy that previous approaches typically require multiple

steps and complex protocols to achieve high fracture resistance. In contrast, our strategy is a simple

one-pot process—requiring only mixing and curing—making it scalable and practical for mass

production.

Next, we test different types of oligomers to study the conditions for the formation of

ESSs. We prepare two more supramolecular stickers in addition to MPU: hexamethylene diurea

(HU) and isophorone diurea (IU) (Fig. 3a). These supramolecular stickers have two urea functional

groups that can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Thus, on average, an MPU forms quadruple

hydrogen bonds with two urea groups. In the case of IU, however, two urea groups cannot form

hydrogen bonds simultaneously because of the bulky isophorone group. In the case of HU, the

hexamethylene group can freely rotate, which increases the entropic penalty and makes the

hydrogen bonds less stable (Supplementary Fig. 6)30. Therefore, the oligomers with MPU will self-

assemble into nanofibers, compared to the others.

We synthesize oligomers with three types of stickers and study their self-assembly in

solution by measuring viscosity as a function of oligomer concentration (Fig. 3b). As expected

from the molecular structures, IU and HU oligomers need higher concentrations to assemble into

supramolecules compared to the MPU oligomers. Also, the sticker has a profound impact on the

morphology of the supramolecules. The AFM images of the assembled oligomers spin-coated on

a silicon wafer show that MPU oligomers form nanofibers, whereas IU and HU oligomers do not

form nanofibers (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 7). The TEM images of the cross-section of the

assembled oligomers show that MPU forms porous nanosized ESS, whereas IU do not form large

domains and HU oligomers form a bicontinuous phase (Supplementary Fig. 8). We attribute these

observations to the absence of the cooperative hydrogen bonds that stabilize the ESSs in the

precursor solution.

The nanofiber structure is crucial for creating distinct ESS with a wide range of

concentrations. Next, we polymerize the ethyl acrylate precursor containing the oligomers and

study their mechanical properties (Fig. 3d). The PEAs with IU oligomers and HU oligomers

exhibit much lower strength than the ESS-PEA, suggesting that the ESSs homogenize the tension

and strengthen the polymer network. Furthermore, we find that the number of stickers of the MPU

oligomer also affects mechanical properties (Extended Data Fig. 7). The spacer chains separating

the interlinks and stickers are also essential to form ESSs. When the oligomers do not have spacer


<!-- Page 17 -->


15

chains, they agglomerate and precipitate due to excessive interchain interaction, whereas

oligomers with the spacer chains form nanosized ESSs that can be dispersed in the precursor

solution (Fig. 3e). This observation suggests that the supramolecular interaction and dissolution of

oligomers are required to be balanced to form stable ESSs.

Our ESS system is universally applicable to other acrylate monomer systems. We

introduce ESSs into various acrylate monomers, such as hexyl methacrylate and butyl acrylate,

and polymerize them. The resulting polymer networks with ESS also show a significant increase

in fracture strength (Fig. 3f and 3g). We also synthesize oligomers for hydrophilic polymer

networks or hydrogels by replacing PDMS chains with hydrophilic spacer chains, while

maintaining the structure of stickers (Supplementary Fig. 9). The synthesized oligomers form

hydrophilic ESSs in the precursor of hydrophilic polymer networks. Specifically, we synthesize

two hydrophilic materials: oligomers using polypropylene glycol (ESSPPG) with 2-hydroxyethyl

acrylate (HEA) and oligomers using polyethylene glycol (ESSPEG) with acrylamide (AAm). After

polymerization, ESSPPG-PHEA shows a markedly lower contact angle compared to that of ESS-

PEA, indicating high hydrophilicity (Fig. 3h). Also, both ESSPPG-PHEA and ESSPEG-PAAm

exhibit a significant increase in strength (Fig. 3i, 3j; Supplementary Fig. 10; and Supplementary

Video 1).

We also test the effects of ESSs in a polymer network with a high glass transition

temperature, such as poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA). The PMMA containing the ESSs shows

a significant increase in the stretchability and strength (Fig. 3k), which is also demonstrated in the

ball impact test (Fig. 3l; Supplementary Fig. 11; and Supplementary Video 2). Furthermore, the

ESSs toughen the polymer networks (Fig. 3m). The ESS-PMMA is tougher than PMMA by 91

times, and other elastomers and hydrogels are also toughened manifolds by ESSs. For example,


<!-- Page 18 -->


16

the ESS-PHEA shows a toughness of about 10,000 J/m2, which is 2.3 times higher than pristine

PHEA.

The formation of polymer networks via free-radical polymerization is highly sensitive to

initiator concentration.47,48 At low initiator concentrations (<0.1 wt%), the backbone chains are

long and densely entangled, providing outstanding fracture resistance, but the curing time is

relatively long. In contrast, high initiator concentrations enable rapid curing but often yield poor

mechanical properties due to short polymer chains. Such a tradeoff between curing rate and

fracture resistance limits the rapid processing of fracture-resistant polymer networks. In our studies,

we find that ESS not only homogenizes the tension but also promotes the percolation of polymer

chains, resolving the tradeoff. To study the effects of ESS on gelation time, we measure the

rheological properties of the butyl acrylate precursor during the curing process. At a wide range of

initiator concentrations, the precursors with ESS gelate faster than those without ESS (Fig. 4a, b

and Extended Data Fig. 8). Note that the gelation time rapidly increases at high initiator

concentrations over 2 wt% due to the short backbone length. In contrast, ESSs enable gelation at

such high initiator concentrations. Also, after curing, the precursors with ESS exhibit higher

storage modulus than those without ESS (Fig. 4c). We attribute the faster gelation and higher

modulus to the many covalent and topological interlinks of ESSs. Finally, we measure the fracture

strength of samples with various curing times (Fig. 4d). The ESS accelerates gelation and rapidly

strengthens the pristine network, resolving the tradeoff between curing time and fracture resistance

(Supplementary Fig. 12 and 13).

Overcoming this tradeoff opens new possibilities in the development of high-performance

photocurable resins for light-based 3D printing46,49–51. We prepare the photocurable ESS resin for

digital light processing (DLP) using ESSPPG-PHEA. Compared to commercial resins such as IBT

Flex Resin (Formlabs) and polyurethane (PU) resin, the ESS resin can build 3D structures more

rapidly (Fig. 4e) with the spatial resolution of ~0.7 mm (Fig. 4f and g). Simultaneously, the 3D

structures printed from the ESS resin show great fracture resistance, as demonstrated by the cyclic

loading tests (Fig. 4h and i, and Supplementary Video 3).

We present a new principle that can achieve an ultralong lifetime of soft materials by

utilizing elastic supramolecular sponges (ESS). To form ESS, we design and synthesize oligomers

that can self-assemble into mesoscale, compliant, and elastic structures. The ESSs are covalently

and topologically interlinked with the polymer network, such that the stress is deconcentrated due

to the elastic deformation of ESSs. Such a homogenization of tension enhances the fracture and

fatigue resistance while maintaining elasticity, which contrasts with existing toughening strategies

that typically compromise elasticity. Our principle is applicable to various material systems and

broad ranges of initiators and crosslinkers, highlighting the generality of the principle. We expect

our principle can be expanded for designing conductive ionogels, functional nanocomposites, and

self-healing polymers. We also demonstrate the utility of our principle to light-based 3D printing,

achieving 2D and 3D structures with exceptional elasticity, fracture strength, and fatigue resistance.

Integration with 3D printing technology is expected to enable the rapid processing of electronic


<!-- Page 21 -->


19

skins and soft robots by allowing the fabrication of more complex structures with high spatial

resolution.

## Methods

Synthetic protocols

Synthesis of MPU Oligomer. A 250 mL 2-neck round bottom flask was charged with H2N-

PDMS-NH2 (20.0 g, ~ 4.00 mmol) and dry DCM (80 mL) under argon atmosphere. To this mixture,

DCM (10 mL) solution of MDPI (0.75 g, 3.0 mmol) was added dropwise via syringe over a period

of 60 min. The solution was stirred at room temperature for additional 2 hours under argon

atmosphere. Then, 2-isocyanatoethyl methacrylate (0.70 mL, 5.0 mmol) was added and the

resulting solution was further stirred at room temperature for 6 hours under dark condition to

complete the reaction. Then, MeOH (1 mL) was added to quench the reaction, and the resulting

solution was concentrated in vacuo. The residue was dissolved in a minimal amount of DCM and

an excess amount of MeOH was added to induce precipitation. After 30 min, the supernatant liquid

fraction was decanted to afford polymer precipitates. This dissolution–precipitation–decantation

process was repeated twice, and the resulting precipitates were completely dried under reduced

pressure for three hours at 35 °C to afford MPU oligomer. As a result, MPU oligomer (13 g) was

obtained. 1H NMR (500 MHz, THF-d8, 298 K): δ 7.29 (d, J = 7.9 Hz, 12H), δ 6.95 (d, J = 8.1 Hz,

12H), δ 6.06 (m, 2H), δ 5.54 (m, 2H), δ 4.10 (t, J = 5.7 Hz, 4H), δ 3.77 (s, 6H), δ 3.36 (m, 4H), δ

3.13 (m, 12H), δ 3.06 (m, 4H), δ 1.91 (s, 6H), δ 1.52 (m, 16H), δ 0.56 (m, 16H), δ 0.11 (s, 1215H).

Synthesis of MPU oligomer without interlink. Synthetic protocol for MPU oligomer without

interlink was identical with that for MPU oligomer except for the use of hexyl isocyanate (0.73

mL, 5.0 mmol) instead of 2-isocyanatoethyl methacrylate (0.70 mL, 5.0 mmol). As a result, MPU

oligomer without interlink (13 g) was obtained. 1H NMR (500 MHz, THF-d8, 298 K): δ 7.28 (d,


<!-- Page 28 -->


26

J = 8.4 Hz, 12H), δ 6.95 (d, J = 8.5 Hz, 12H), δ 3.77 (s, 5H), δ 3.13 (m, 11H), δ 3.06 (m, 7H), δ

1.52 (m, 11H), δ 1.44 (m, 8H), δ 0.89 (m, 11H), δ 0.56 (m, 15H), δ 0.11 (s, 1203H).

Preparation of polymer networks (Fig. 2)

ESS-PEA. MPU oligomer (0.2 g) was dissolved in ethyl acrylate (1984 μL) to obtain a 9.5 wt%

solution. A TDDA stock solution was separately prepared by dissolving TDDA (0.01 g) in DMF

(100 μL), from which 28 μL was taken and added to the first solution. A photoinitiator stock

solution was separately prepared by dissolving I-2959 photoinitiator (0.01 g) in DMF (1 mL), from

which 14.9 μL was taken and added to the first solution. For mold preparation,

Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tape was attached to a 7 cm × 10 cm glass plate to serve as the

mold and cover, and polyethylene terephthalate (PET, 300 μm) was used as a spacer. The mixed

solution was then poured into the mold and sealed with the cover. The mold, spacer, and cover

were clamped tightly, and the sample was cured under a 40 W, 365 nm UV lamp (VILBER, Bio-

Link) for 12 hr.

ESS-PEA w/o interlink. The preparation of ESS-PEA w/o interlink was identical to that of ESS-

PEA, except that MPU oligomer without interlinks was used instead of MPU oligomer.

PEA. The preparation of PEA was identical to that of ESS-PEA, except that the MPU oligomer

was omitted.

Mechanical characterization

Tensile, fracture, fatigue and puncture tests were conducted using a universal testing machine

(UTM) (Instron 68SC-1).


<!-- Page 29 -->


27

Uniaxial tensile tests. Tensile tests were performed under ambient conditions with dogbone shape

specimens. The central dimension of the dogbone samples were 1.5 mm × 15 mm (width × length)

and the loading rate was 300 mm min–1 (2000% min–1).

Toughness tests. Notched specimens for fracture and fatigue tests were prepared by cutting the

polymer films into rectangular shape (35 mm × 10 mm), with the length of the notch being half of

the width. Fracture tests were performed with the loading rate of 200 mm min–1 (2000% min–1).

Fatigue tests. For fatigue tests, we first prepared a rectangular sample having a width of 35 mm

and a height of 10 mm. Then, we applied a cyclic loading to the sample with a given stretch

amplitude (𝜆௔௠௣௟). The stretch rate was 200 mm min−1. After ~ 3,000 cycles, the stress-stretch

curve reached the steady state. From the stress-stretch curve ߪ(𝜆) at the steady state, we calculated

an energy release rate ܩ= ܪ× ∫ ߪ(𝜆) ఒೌ೘೛೗ 0 ݀𝜆, where ܪ is the initial height of the sample. Then,

we cut a notch with a length of 17.5 mm on the rectangular sample and marked the position of the

crack tip. After applying ܰ = 10,000 cycles of cyclic loading at the stretch amplitude 𝜆௔௠௣௟  and

the stretch rate of 200 mm min−1, we measured the crack advance ܿ by an optical microscope

(Nikon ECLIPSE LV100N POL). The crack growth per cycle ݀ܿ/݀ܰ was calculated by ܿ/ܰ, by

assuming that ܿ linearly increases in ܰ. We measured the energy release rate and the crack growth

rate at different values of the stretch amplitude. The crack growth rate was plotted against the

energy release rate, and the fatigue threshold was determined by linear interpolation.

Rheology measurements under UV

The change in modulus over UV curing time was measured using a rheometer (Anton Paar, MCR

302) with a 25 mm-diameter parallel plate. 405 nm UV light was exposed through the bottom plate

composed of quartz. The gap between parallel plates was fixed to 0.1 mm and ~50 μL of resin was


<!-- Page 30 -->


28

loaded for each measurement. The amplitude of shear strain was set to 1% and the frequency was

set to 1 Hz.

Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS)

SAXS experiments were conducted at the 4C SAXS Ⅱ beamline52 located at the Pohang

Accelerator Laboratory (PAL) in Pohang, Republic of Korea. Storage ring energy was 3.0 GeV,

and the sample-to-detector distances were set at 4 m, 1 m, and 20 cm. To obtain 2D SAXS profiles

for stretched films, a stretcher was set on the stage between the beam source and the detector.

Polymer films were stretched by the stretcher, and anchored on the stage and the position of the

stage was controlled to ensure that the beam always pass through the middle of the specimen.

3D printing

To prepare the ESS resin for 3D printing, 12.5 g of MPU oligomer with PPG backbone and 131

mg of TDDA were dissolved in 50 g of HEA. Then 0.313 g of photoinitiator (diphenyl(2,4,6-

trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide, TPO) was added to the mixed solution. This solution served as

a photocurable resin without additional heating process. 3D printing was carried out with a digital

light processing (DLP) printer (ASIGA, MAX X27) with a UV LED wavelength of 385 nm. The

layer thickness was set to 100 μm. The light intensity and irradiation time for curing each layer

were set to 3 mW cm–2 and 3 s, respectively. The 3D printed objects were immersed in ethanol

and sonicated for 60 s to wash out residual resins.
